<reason>PRO (Side B) built the clearer path to victory. Its core move—seizing CON's [A1.3] distinction ("unfair on who develops ability, meritocratic on selecting it") and arguing that faithfully certifying purchased preparation is exactly what "reproducing class privilege" means—was never squarely neutralized. CON's mechanisms for breaking the chain in A1 (need-based aid, recruitment beyond networks) were thin, and CON itself conceded that a pathway mostly recruiting affluent candidates "can reproduce advantage." PRO also gave a clean operational test in its A1 (class "decides" if it still predicts outcomes among the equally qualified) with concrete post-floor mechanisms, directly answering CON's pressure question. CON's strongest line—that PRO shows inequality's existence but not the required comparison between actual and admitted contribution—was coherent and epistemically disciplined, but PRO answered it in closing by locating the overstatement in the gap between the standard meritocratic narrative and CON's own account of the machinery. CON's "emphasis isn't misrepresentation" point had some force, but PRO's "defense of silence" reply and the framing that the motion asks what people admit, not whether they deny, landed. PRO's clipped opening and mild burden-shifting ("if fuller admissions were common CON would cite them") were minor costs. Overall a clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B2.1]–[B2.5] turning CON's two-stage distinction into a concession ("the exam does not launder the first stage; it certifies it") and pressing "developed by whom, with what money?"—which CON never fully escaped, ending up conceding in [A4.1] that such pathways "can reproduce advantage."</best_rebuttal>
